content: Hot flushes are the most prevalent vasomotor symptom experienced during menopause. Hormone therapy (HT) has traditionally been recommended to alleviate these symptoms. However, due to concerns regarding the potential health risks associated with HT, many women have sought alternative treatments. Acupuncture has been proposed as a potential method to reduce the frequency and severity of hot flushes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in reducing hot flushes and improving the quality of life in menopausal women experiencing vasomotor symptoms. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted in January 2013 to identify relevant studies. These databases included the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and several Chinese medical literature databases, among others. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any form of acupuncture to either no treatment, a control group, or other treatments for menopausal hot flushes. Sixteen studies involving a total of 1,155 women met the inclusion criteria. Three independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the data. Where appropriate, data were pooled, and mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The overall quality of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE criteria. Eight studies compared acupuncture to sham acupuncture. There was no significant difference between the two groups in terms of hot flush frequency (MD -1.13 flushes per day, 95% CI -2.55 to 0.29; 8 RCTs, 414 women; I² = 70%; low-quality evidence). However, the severity of hot flushes was significantly lower in the acupuncture group, with a small effect size (SMD -0.45, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.05; 6 RCTs, 297 women; I² = 62%; very low-quality evidence). Substantial heterogeneity was observed in both outcomes. A post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding studies involving women with breast cancer reduced heterogeneity to 0% for hot flush frequency and 34% for hot flush severity, but no significant differences were found between the groups for either outcome. Three studies compared acupuncture to HT. Women in the acupuncture group experienced significantly more frequent hot flushes than those in the HT group (MD 3.18 flushes per day, 95% CI 2.06 to 4.29; 3 RCTs, 114 women; I² = 0%; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference between the groups in terms of hot flush severity (SMD 0.53, 95% CI -0.14 to 1.20; 2 RCTs, 84 women; I² = 57%; low-quality evidence). One study compared electroacupuncture to relaxation therapy. No significant differences were observed between the two groups for either hot flush frequency (MD -0.40 flushes per day, 95% CI -2.18 to 1.38; 1 RCT, 38 women; very low-quality evidence) or hot flush severity (MD 0.20, 95% CI -0.85 to 1.25; 1 RCT, 38 women; very low-quality evidence). Four studies compared acupuncture to a waiting list or no intervention. Traditional acupuncture was significantly more effective in reducing hot flush frequency from baseline (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.31; 3 RCTs, 463 women; I² = 0%; low-quality evidence) and in reducing hot flush severity (SMD -0.54, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.35; 3 RCTs, 463 women; I² = 0%; low-quality evidence). The effect size was moderate in both cases. In terms of quality of life, acupuncture was significantly less effective than HT. However, traditional acupuncture was significantly more effective than no intervention. There were no significant differences between acupuncture and other comparators for quality of life outcomes. Data on adverse effects were insufficient. In conclusion, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether acupuncture is effective for managing menopausal vasomotor symptoms. When compared to sham acupuncture, no significant differences were observed in the effects on menopausal symptoms. Acupuncture appeared to be beneficial when compared to no treatment, but it was less effective than HT. These findings should be interpreted with caution due to the low or very low quality of the evidence and the lack of sham acupuncture or placebo HT controls in studies comparing acupuncture to no treatment or HT. Data on adverse effects were lacking.
